lead: An engine is described with a small fixed set of words: bore, stroke, top dead centre, bottom dead centre, swept volume, clearance volume, compression ratio and mean effective pressure. Every later calculation — power, efficiency, torque — is built from these. The same engine has a fixed set of parts, each with one job and a material chosen for that job. This chapter gives both lists, so that later chapters can use the words and the parts without re-defining them.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for what an IC engine is, and school geometry for the area of a circle and the volume of a cylinder.

sections.h3: The geometry words every later formula uses

blocks.text: These six words describe the space inside one cylinder. Fix them now; later chapters assume them.

items: Bore (d): the inside diameter of the cylinder, in mm or cm.
Stroke (L): the distance the piston travels from its highest to its lowest position. Stroke equals twice the crank radius.
Top dead centre (TDC): the piston position closest to the cylinder head. Bottom dead centre (BDC): the position farthest from it.
Swept volume (Vs): the volume the piston sweeps in one stroke, from TDC to BDC.
Clearance volume (Vc): the small volume left above the piston when it is at TDC.
Compression ratio (r): the total cylinder volume at BDC divided by the total volume at TDC.

blocks.where: Vₛ is the swept volume of one cylinder; d is the bore and L is the stroke, both in the same unit (cm gives cm³).
r is the compression ratio, a pure number with no unit; Vₛ is swept volume and Vᴄ is clearance volume, in the same unit.
MEP is mean effective pressure in Pa (divide by 10⁵ for bar); Wₙₑₜ is the net work per cycle in J; Vₛ is swept volume in m³. For a multi-cylinder engine use the total swept volume.

blocks.text: Mean effective pressure is a convenience. It pretends the varying gas pressure inside the cylinder is one steady pressure that would produce the same work in one stroke. It lets you compare a small fast engine with a large slow one on a fair basis, and it is the number an engine tester reports.

sections.h3: The parts, their one job, and their usual material

blocks.text: Group the parts by job and the list stops feeling long. One group holds everything together, one takes the gas pressure, one delivers the output, one controls gas flow, and one smooths the rotation.

blocks.text: Timing of the valves and the order in which cylinders fire are separate topics; see Chapter 1.5 and Chapter 1.6.

sections.h3: Why these materials and not others

blocks.text: Each material answers one hard demand.

items: The piston must be light, because it reverses direction twice per revolution. Aluminium alloy weighs about one third of cast iron for the same size, so the reversing forces stay small.
The crankshaft must be stiff and strong, because it carries the full torque of every cylinder at once. Forged alloy steel is used, and the journals are ground smooth for the bearings.
The block must be rigid, cheap and good at damping vibration. Cast iron does all three; aluminium alloy saves weight but needs steel liners where the piston slides.
The exhaust valve runs red hot and must not soften. Alloy steels with chromium and silicon keep their strength at high temperature.
Rings must press against the bore and still slide. Cast iron or steel keeps its springiness at working temperature.

blocks.text: The gap between the piston and the bore is set for the hottest running condition. A cold engine is therefore slightly noisy, and a Chennai engine started on a cool morning sounds different from the same engine after a highway run.

examples.question: A four-cylinder engine has a bore of 80 mm, a stroke of 90 mm and a clearance volume of 62.8 cm³ per cylinder. Find the swept volume of one cylinder, the total displacement, and the compression ratio.
steps: Convert the lengths to centimetres so that the volume comes out in cm³: bore d = 80 mm = 8.0 cm, stroke L = 90 mm = 9.0 cm.
Swept volume of one cylinder: Vₛ = (π/4) d² L = 0.7854 × (8.0)² × 9.0 = 0.7854 × 64.0 × 9.0 = 452.4 cm³.
Total displacement for four cylinders: 4 × 452.4 = 1809.6 cm³, that is about 1.81 litre. This is the number a car brochure calls 1.8 L.
Check the units: cm³ divided by cm³ leaves a pure number, so r = 8.20 has no unit.
examples.answer: Swept volume = 452.4 cm³ per cylinder, total displacement = 1809.6 cm³ (≈ 1.81 L), and compression ratio = 8.20.
examples.check:
import math
d = 8.0        # bore in cm
L = 9.0        # stroke in cm
Vc = 62.8      # clearance volume per cylinder in cm3
n = 4          # number of cylinders
Vs = math.pi / 4 * d**2 * L
Vt = n * Vs
r = (Vs + Vc) / Vc
print(round(Vs, 1))
print(round(Vt, 1))
print(round(r, 2))

traps: Compression ratio is not Vₛ / Vᴄ. It is (Vₛ + Vᴄ) / Vᴄ, because the gas is squeezed into the clearance volume plus nothing else, but it starts from the whole cylinder volume.
Mixing millimetres and centimetres in (π/4) d² L. A bore of 80 mm is 8.0 cm, not 80. Square the bore in the unit you will use for the stroke.
Swept volume is one cylinder; total displacement is swept volume times the number of cylinders. The example gives both, and examiners often ask only one.
Stroke is twice the crank radius, not the crank radius. A common slip in balance and piston-speed sums.
Mean effective pressure needs swept volume in m³ to give pascals. Feed it cm³ and your answer is out by a factor of one million.

quiz.q: Define bore and stroke, and give the unit of each.
quiz.a: Bore is the inside diameter of the cylinder; stroke is the distance the piston moves from TDC to BDC. Both are lengths, usually quoted in mm.

quiz.q: Name the usual material for the piston, the connecting rod and the cylinder block.
quiz.a: Piston: aluminium alloy with silicon. Connecting rod: forged steel. Cylinder block: cast iron, or aluminium alloy in small engines.

quiz.q: Why is the piston made of aluminium alloy rather than cast iron?
quiz.a: The piston reverses direction twice per revolution, so its mass matters. Aluminium alloy is about one third as dense as cast iron, which keeps the reversing inertia force small at high speed. It also conducts heat away from the crown faster. Cast iron is used only where weight matters less.

quiz.q: Explain why compression ratio has no unit.
quiz.a: It is a ratio of two volumes, (Vₛ + Vᴄ) to Vᴄ, measured in the same unit. The units cancel, so r is a pure number. That is why we write r = 8.2 and not 8.2 cm³.

quiz.q: A single-cylinder engine has a bore of 100 mm, a stroke of 120 mm and a clearance volume of 100 cm³. Find the swept volume and the compression ratio.
An engine of total displacement 1.81 L develops a net indicated work of 700 J per cycle. Find the mean effective pressure in bar.
quiz.a: Use total swept volume Vₛ = 1.81 L = 1.81 × 10⁻³ m³. MEP = W / Vₛ = 700 / 0.00181 = 386 740 Pa. Divide by 10⁵: MEP ≈ 3.87 bar.

quiz.q: A student computes the compression ratio of the worked example as 452.4 / 62.8 = 7.20. State what went wrong, give the correct value, and say which engine runs hotter, r = 7.20 or r = 8.20.
quiz.a: The student divided swept volume by clearance volume and left out the clearance volume in the numerator. The cylinder volume at BDC is Vₛ + Vᴄ, so r = 515.2 / 62.8 = 8.20. The higher ratio, 8.20, compresses the charge into a smaller space and gives a higher temperature and pressure at the end of compression, so that engine runs hotter.

quiz.q: Explain why the clearance volume of a real engine can never be zero, and what would break if it were.
quiz.a: The clearance space holds the valves, the spark plug or injector, and the gas at TDC. If it were zero, the piston would strike the head, the gas would be pushed out, and there would be no room for combustion to start. The compression ratio would be infinite and the pressure rise would destroy the parts. In practice a minimum clearance also covers thermal expansion of the piston and rod.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the same vocabulary carries into computer models: a mesh for the cylinder is built from exactly bore, stroke and clearance volume. Materials have moved on too — many blocks are now aluminium with pressed-in liners, and pistons carry a steel insert in the top ring groove so the groove does not wear out. Search next for 'engine geometry parameters', 'piston alloy 4032' and 'cylinder liner materials' if you want the design side.
